questions.prompt: Which modern C++20 utility reinterprets the bit pattern of a float as a std::uint32_t safely and supports constexpr evaluation?
options: std::launder<std::uint32_t>(f)
*reinterpret_cast<std::uint32_t*>(&f)
std::assume_aligned<4>(f)
std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(f)
questions.explanation: std::bit_cast<To>(from) in <bit> creates a new To value from the object representation of from without aliasing pointers, requires matching sizes and trivially copyable types, and works in constexpr.

questions.prompt: Why does reading an inactive member of a union (such as writing u.f = 1.0f; and reading u.i;) invoke undefined behavior in C++?
options: At most one union member can be active at a time in C++, so reading an inactive member breaks object lifetime rules
Unions cannot store floating-point and integer types together
Designated initializers always zero-initialize the wrong member
Reading p.u violates alignment rules on 64-bit targets
questions.explanation: Unlike C99/C11 where union type punning is valid, C++ unions ([class.union]) have at most one active member whose lifetime is active. Accessing p.u when p.f is active is UB (save for the narrow common-initial-sequence rule for standard-layout structs).

questions.prompt: In the function below, why can an optimizing compiler legally delete the `if (!p)` check?
options: Pointers passed as function arguments can never be null in C++
The compiler caches `int v` in a register before evaluating `!p`
Dereferencing *p on line 1 would be UB if p were null, allowing the optimizer to deduce p != nullptr
The optimizer treats return -1 as unreachable for non-negative integers
questions.explanation: Because *p precedes if (!p), any execution with p == nullptr already triggered undefined behavior. Under [intro.abstract], the optimizer assumes UB never happens, proves p != nullptr after line 1, and removes the dead branch.

questions.prompt: Assuming `int buf[4]{};`, which pointer formation alone triggers undefined behavior even if you never dereference the resulting pointer?
options: int* end = buf + 4;
int* bad = buf + 5;
int* first = &buf[0];
void* raw = buf;
questions.explanation: Under [expr.add], pointer arithmetic is defined only within the array bounds plus one-past-the-end (buf + 4). Forming buf + 5—or buf - 1—causes undefined behavior immediately upon pointer addition, even without dereferencing.

questions.prompt: According to [basic.lval]/11, which byte-oriented pointer type is NOT listed as permitted to alias an object of an arbitrary dynamic type like double?
options: char*
unsigned char*
std::byte*
signed char*
questions.explanation: Section [basic.lval]/11 explicitly grants byte-level aliasing to char, unsigned char, and std::byte—never signed char! Using signed char* (or int8_t*) to inspect arbitrary object representations violates strict aliasing.

questions.prompt: Under [class.mem.general], when is reading an inactive member of a standard-layout union well-defined in C++?
options: When accessing a member belonging to the common initial sequence of two standard-layout struct members of the union
Whenever both struct members have identical total sizeof
Only when the union is declared inside an extern "C" block
Whenever the member is read through a reinterpret_cast
questions.explanation: Per [class.mem.general], in a standard-layout union with active member of struct type T1, it is permitted to inspect a non-static data member m of another standard-layout struct member T2 provided m belongs to their common initial sequence (like int tag above).
